title: A monogrammed travel case — and a letter that doesn't hold up
body: A Victorian burl-walnut travel and dressing case, held in a private US collection, with cut-crystal jars, silver-lidded boxes and a mother-of-pearl lid plaque. The silver lids carry an engraved monogram reading M·K·W — the Victorian convention of centring the surname initial is consistent with Myles Walter Keogh. The collector, who has asked to remain unnamed, gave permission in July 2026 for these photographs to be published.

An accompanying letter, undated but claimed as 1915, tells a story of the case being handed down by a Fort Abraham Lincoln stable boy after Keogh's death. That letter cannot be relied upon as written: it invokes Michael Collins as a fundraising figurehead (not associated with Irish-American fundraising until 1919 at the earliest), refers to Ireland as "Eire" (an English-usage form dating from the 1937 Constitution), and uses "Brits" as a pejorative — a usage that belongs to the Troubles era, decades later. Whatever the case's real history, this letter is not a reliable record of it.
Shown here for transparency rather than as evidence. The object may or may not have any real connection to Keogh; the letter attached to it does not establish one.

quote: When I was 7 or 8 I was stabling and grooming at Fort Abraham Lincoln. Mr. Keogh and I got along well since we were both of Eire. After the slaughter of Mr. Keogh in June of '76 the men left behind gave to me Mr. Keogh's personal travel set he [had] left at the fort... Now that Michael Collins is raising monies to free my homeland of the [bastard] Brits, Mr. Keogh would want me to sell his box for him. Paid in full. — Patrick Sean Donnel[ly]

title: The woman at the grave — Rhode Island, 1976
body: On the centenary of Keogh's death — 25 June 1976 — a cemetery worker at Fort Hill Cemetery, Auburn, reported that an elderly woman had visited his grave that morning, arriving by chauffeur-driven car with Rhode Island licence plates.

title: Martin family papers — Willowbrook
body: The Throop-Martin family of Auburn, New York were Keogh's surrogate family for the last decade of his life. He described their estate, Willowbrook, as "a second home to me."

Keogh's last letter was addressed to Nelly Martin in October 1875. Lenora Snedeker's Memories at Willowbrook (Oxford, NY, 1995) is the primary published source on the family. Cayuga County Historical Society is the likely archive.

title: Letters in family possession, 1861–1875
body: The Dictionary of Irish Biography records that "some Keogh letters and papers, covering the period 1861–75, are in the possession of the family." Orchard House is still occupied by the Keogh family.
The 2008 Kimber–Doyle visit to Orchard House confirmed a substantial family file held by Miley Keogh. Current status of the archive requires confirmation.

title: The satchel — Mrs Eliza Porter, Fort Lincoln, 1876
body: Before the Little Bighorn campaign, Keogh left a satchel of personal papers with Mrs Eliza Porter, wife of Company I's Lieutenant James Porter.
Whether the instruction was carried out — and whether any material survived — is not confirmed. Mrs Porter's own papers and letters are a research priority.
quote: He instructed her to burn them should he be killed.

title: Papal Army records — Archivio di Stato, Rome
body: Records of the Battalion of St Patrick and the broader Papal Army of 1860 are held in Italian state archives. The Holy See's records for the Pro Petri Sede medal and Order of St Gregory recipients are maintained by the Association of Papal Orders.
Keogh's replacement medals (after the originals were lost in the Galt House Hotel fire, Louisville, 1865) were obtained in 1867.

title: Hayes-McCoy monograph, NUI Galway (1965)
body: G.A. Hayes-McCoy, Captain Myles Walter Keogh, United States Army 1840–1876. O'Donnell Lecture, National University of Ireland, Galway, 1965.

A full-length scholarly study predating the Langellier/Cox/Pohanka volume by 26 years. The most focused Irish academic treatment of Keogh's career. Held at NUI Galway library and the National Library of Ireland.

title: School roll — Leighlinbridge National School
body: The enrolment register of Leighlinbridge National School survives in the Keogh family archive at Orchard House. Keogh appears as "Miles Kehoe," pupil no. 201, enrolled 1 May 1848.
Schoolmaster: John Conwill. Rapid progress through the curriculum — at Level 5 Reading by July 1852, attained by only three other pupils.

title: Keogh Family Papers — Autry Museum, Los Angeles
body: The Autry Museum of the American West holds the principal collection of documents returned to Keogh's family in Ireland after his death. Two albums: one of original documents and photographs, one a letter book relating to his service record.
Commission papers, citizenship documents (1869), passport (1869), the Sturgis order regarding Comanche (April 1878), and six photographs of Keogh in uniform.
